Title: BadBox 3.0 Ad Fraud Operation Generating 40 Billion Daily Bid Requests Disrupted
Context: The first BadBox botnet ensnared more than 190,000 devices, while BadBox 2
Full Text:
Bot and fraud protection firm Human Security says it has disrupted the largest ad fraud botnet by bid volume.

Dubbed BadBox 3.0, it is the third iteration of a large operation targeting low-cost Android devices. The first BadBox botnet ensnared more than 190,000 devices, while BadBox 2.0 was initially found on over 1 million devices, but eventually ensnared more than 10 million.

“At its height, BadBox 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform,” Human Security says, noting the bid request volume was three times the volume recorded for the VastFlux ad fraud scheme.

Portions of BadBox 3.0, the cybersecurity firm says, were operated via command-and-control (C&C) domains that were disrupted when Google took down XCPE, a botnet of over 1.3 million Android set-top boxes.

The botnet consists of low-cost, uncertified Android Open Source Project devices infected with backdoors delivering fraud modules designed to render hidden video ads and to enroll the devices into residential proxy networks.

Human Security says its Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team has uncovered an actively maintained catalog of fraud modules hosted on public repositories, as well as links to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ. Some of the modules were previously seen in BadBox and BadBox 2.0.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Most modules in the catalog are residential proxy modules and the droppers that install them, but the collection also carries new ad fraud modules, and researchers traced both payloads to the same infrastructure and code,” Human Security notes.

Mimicking video ad software development kits (SDKs), the botnet’s ad fraud modules render ads in a hidden window, making the bid requests appear as coming from known, legitimate apps that the threat actors impersonated.

While the device owner does not see the ads, the supply chain sees a premium CTV inventory consisting of well-known applications that likely aren’t even installed on the infected devices, along with residential IP addresses and full video ads. In some cases, the threat actors relied on server-side ad insertion (SSAI) to monetize application spoofing.

“The volume reached roughly 40 billion bid requests a day, and much of it arrived from IP addresses associated with residential proxy networks, which helped it pass as ordinary household viewing,” Human Security notes.

Proxyjacking modules deployed on the same devices enrolled them in eleven residential proxy networks, including a rebranded version of IpMoYu, now named PXYEDGE, the network operated by the threat actors behind BadBox and BadBox 2.0.

Human Security has found several links between BadBox 3.0 and the Chinese company TXCZ: the modules check for TXCZ build properties, a TXCZ domain serves payload download routes and configurations for the hidden ads, and Human linked TXCZ to repositories distributing ad fraud launchers.

In addition to public repositories, the threat actor uses a second code platform and a file server to host payloads. For some payloads, it also uses a free open-source CDN that mirrors public repositories. The operators also use a self-hosted GitHub proxy.

Human Security has not provided an estimated size of BadBox 3.0, but noted that the mirror for one repository served over 367,000 requests over a month, which does not reflect the number of infections.

“These are requests rather than unique devices, and some come from researchers and scanners. It should be made very clear: these numbers are only for one repository, and only of the third backup delivery mechanism. The actual number of BADBOX 3.0 infections can be presumed to be significantly higher,” the cybersecurity firm notes.

Title: Badbox Returns to Spread Ad Fraud and Proxyjacking Payloads
Context: These networks route internet traffic through regular consumer devices and are often abused by threat actors for account takeover, brute-force attacks, malware distribution, and...
Full Text:
Security researchers say they have uncovered what may be the largest ad fraud operation ever discovered by bid volume.

Human’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team claimed Badbox 3.0 accounted for 40 billion bid requests per day at its height, more than three times the previous record holder VastFlux.

“Badbox 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that Human researchers recognized from Badbox and Badbox 2.0,” a report published on November 19 explained.

“Those modules come from an actively maintained catalog hosted on public code repositories. Satori researchers have linked these repositories to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer.”

Read more on Badbox: Malware-Infected Devices Sold Through Major Retailers

The fraud modules secretly render video ads on owners’ devices, sending ad requests that borrow the identities of legitimate apps. They also enroll the device, without the owner’s knowledge, as an exit node in one of 11 residential proxy networks.

These networks route internet traffic through regular consumer devices and are often abused by threat actors for account takeover, brute-force attacks, malware distribution, and more.

One of these networks, Pxyedge, was identified by Human as IpMoYu, a network operated by the actors behind Badbox and Badbox 2.0.

Advice for Device Owners

Human urged users to choose devices from familiar brands, ensure they are Play Protect-certified, only download apps from official marketplaces, and take action if devices behave strangely.

It said those compromised by Badbox 3.0 are all “low-cost, off-brand, uncertified” devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP); built in China and shipped globally.

However, the report warned that the botherders are likely to adapt again, as they have done with previous iterations of Badbox

“The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record,” it explained.

“Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name. Its ad fraud, hidden on the devices and passed off under the names of legitimate apps, reached a daily volume larger than any ad fraud operation disclosed before it.”

On a more positive note, Human said it was part of an operation to disrupt XCPE, a botnet linked to Badbot 3.0 by shared command-and-control (C2) domains. It boasted more than a million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories before the Google-led industry effort.

Title: Infected TV boxes in BADBOX 3.0 rent out their owners’ home internet
Context: The same boxes also rent out the owner’s home internet connection to residential proxy networks, which threat actors use to make attacks look like household traffic
Full Text:
HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team has disrupted BADBOX 3.0, an operation run mainly from infected low-cost TV boxes that generated roughly 40 billion ad bid requests a day at its peak. That was more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic HUMAN observed and more than three times the volume of VASTFLUX, the previous record holder.

The boxes play video ads in a window the owner never sees, and the requests claim to come from well-known streaming apps that do not run on the device.

The same boxes also rent out the owner’s home internet connection to residential proxy networks, which threat actors use to make attacks look like household traffic. Advertisers may pay for ads that no one watches, and the people guarding accounts and payments may see takeover or carding attempts arriving from what looks like a living room.

BADBOX, found in 2023, was a firmware backdoor on uncertified devices, and HUMAN observed more than 74,000 of them. BADBOX 2.0, in 2025, spanned more than 10 million devices in 222 countries and territories. The 3.0 operators reuse pieces of both, including a proxy network first exposed in 2.0.

A catalog hosted in the open

Infected devices contact a command-and-control server, which returns a list of fraud modules and where to download them. The modules sit on public code repositories, with backups on a second code platform, an operator-controlled file server and, for some, a CDN mirror. The operators also run their own GitHub proxy, so blocking the repositories at the network level does not stop the downloads.

One month of CDN statistics for a single repository showed 367,023 requests and about 482.7 GB served. Those are requests, not unique devices, and cover one repository and one of four delivery routes, so Satori presumes actual infections are significantly higher. Antivirus coverage of the newer modules was effectively absent at the time of analysis.

Ads that look like premium inventory

The ad modules mimic legitimate video ad software and render the ads in a hidden window. To a buyer, the request looks like a well-known app, a residential IP address and a full video ad. The apps sending the requests have no business relationship with the apps they claim to be and do not appear in those apps’ sellers.json or app-ads.txt files, where such files exist.

The traffic still has tells. For one abused app identity, about 40% of requests overall and 80% of US requests came from residential proxy exits. A small set of cheap, uncertified Android device models sent nearly all requests to one family of apps, while ordinary CTV devices spread theirs across many.

Eleven proxy networks

Other modules enroll devices in eleven residential proxy networks: ten commercial services and PXYEDGE, which Satori assesses to be IpMoYu, the network exposed in BADBOX 2.0, under a new name. The PXYEDGE domain was registered March 15, 2026, and reports about 200,000 nodes. The owner pays for the bandwidth while someone else sells access to the address.

A Chinese manufacturer is linked

Satori ties the catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer. Modules check for TXCZ-specific build properties before running, and a TXCZ launcher with system-level permissions comes preinstalled on its devices.

The interface of a TXCZ CTV device (Source: HUMAN)

“The practical guidance for end-users remains the same as in earlier BADBOX-family investigations: choose devices from familiar brands, check whether a device is Play Protect certified, download applications only from official marketplaces, and treat a device that behaves strangely as a device worth retiring,” the researchers noted.

Title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?
Context: NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox
Full Text:
Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post.

Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox.

.NET Assembly Loading

The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks.

The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. I used this API method to bypass VirtualBox process hardening back in 2017, I was able to get to the API through the JScript script engine, culminating in me releasing the generic DotNetToJScript tool.

I’d always assumed this was the limit of bootstrapping arbitrary .NET from a memory buffer. If you tried to load a .NET assembly from a file it’d map it as an image section which would hit any DLL hardening checks and block an unsigned and untrusted binary from loading. However, in a “Doh” moment I realized I’d never verified this behavior to be true, thus I decided to take a look.

The most important function to mapping a .NET assembly into memory seems to be PEImageLayout::Map, which is roughly the following in the version 4 of CLR.DLL which implements the runtime:

PEImageLayout *PEImageLayout::Map(HANDLE file) { PEImageLayout* image = new MappedImageLayout(file); if (!image->Image) { image = new FlatImageLayout(file); } if (image->Image) { if (!PEDecoder::CheckFormat(image->Image)) ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } return image; }

What is interesting is this code creates a MappedImageLayout object based on the file. If that fails it’ll fall back to using a different object, FlatImageLayout. The names kind of give away what they’re doing, but just to be sure let’s look at the implementations of the constructors:

void MappedImageLayout::MappedImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, SEC_IMAGE | PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT) ThrowLastError(); } DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_CONFIG_CI(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } // ... }

The constructor for MappedImageLayout uses the CreateFileMapping API to convert the file handle into a section object. The code passes the SEC_IMAGE flag which instructs the kernel to assume the file is a PE executable and build an image section object including mapping in executable memory pages. Any protections which rely on verifying an image’s signature or location can be notified and take appropriate action. However if the CreateFileMapping call fails the code checks if the last error was not ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT and throws ending the load entirely.

An additional check is made here to check if “Code Integrity” is enforced through the Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) APIs. This checks for the “Dynamic Code Security” code integrity policy being enabled or if a User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) policy is enforced. If it is then an error is thrown ending the loading process. We’ll come back to this check when it becomes relevant.

Assuming the mapping fails with the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT error, then the loading process continues, creating a FlatImageLayout object instead:

void FlatImageLayout::FlatImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { ThrowLastError(); } // ... }

This constructor is simpler, it just calls CreateFileMapping without the SEC_IMAGE flag. Therefore the file is mapped into memory as a data only section. There’s no executable pages, but that doesn’t matter for .NET. The final check, back in the first code snippet verifies that the PE file is valid with a call to PEDecoder::CheckFormat, throwing if it’s not valid.

The take away from this is if we can get .NET to load a valid assembly file, but cause the first call to CreateFileMapping to fail with the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT error we can get it to execute the file from memory. Any protection code which is expecting to check the loaded image section will not see the load and untrusted arbitrary code would be executed.

Note this behavior only seems to work on .NET Framework v4, not the older .NET Framework such as v3.5 and v2. From what I can tell in the earlier frameworks, while this check can be bypassed in the same way and the FlatImageLayout object created, the runtime passes the assembly to the LoadLibrary API later in the loading process where it will fail to load. I didn’t spend much time checking if this was bypassable, as the older .NET Frameworks are no longer installed by default and aren’t even included as optional components in the latest versions of Windows 11. I also didn’t investigate the modern .NET runtimes, v5 and above for similar reasons.

VirtualBox DLL Loading Hooks

Now that we have a potential route to bypassing a process hardening image checker using .NET let’s dig into how it was exploitable in VirtualBox. The previous blog post described how VirtualBox on Windows adds hooks to the DLL loader in order to prevent untrusted images from loading into the process. The important hook for our purposes is the one attached to the NtCreateSection system call which is called under the hood by CreateFileMapping to create the image section object. The following is the start of the hook function:

NTSTATUS supR3HardenedMonitor_NtCreateSection(PHANDLE phSection, ACCESS_MASK fAccess, POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES pObjAttribs, PLARGE_INTEGER pcbSection, ULONG fProtect, ULONG fAttribs, HANDLE hFile) { bool const fExecProt = (fProtect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) != 0; if (hFile != NULL && hFile != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { bool const fImage = RT_BOOL(fAttribs & (SEC_IMAGE | SEC_PROTECTED_IMAGE)); bool const fExecMap = RT_BOOL(fAccess & SECTION_MAP_EXECUTE); if (fImage || fExecMap || fExecProt) { bool fCallRealApi; NTSTATUS rcNt = supR3HardenedScreenImage(hFile, fImage, true /*fIgnoreArch*/, &fAccess, &fProtect, &fCallRealApi, "NtCreateSection", true /*fAvoidWinVerifyTrust*/, NULL /*pfQuiet*/); if (!NT_SUCCESS(rcNt)) return rcNt; if (!fCallRealApi) return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } } NTSTATUS rcNtReal = g_pfnNtCreateSectionReal(phSection, fAccess, pObjAttribs, pcbSection, fProtect, fAttribs, hFile); // ...

If the NtCreateSection call requests an executable section, such as via the SEC_IMAGE flag, then the file is passed to the supR3HardenedScreenImage support API which will check if the PE file matches VirtualBox’s loading criteria, only calling the original NtCreateSection system call if that succeeds or the file is not being mapped as executable. Importantly the CreateFileMapping call in FlatImageLayout would not hit the checks as it doesn’t request an image or executable mapping.

In order for CreateFileMapping to set the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT last error, NtCreateSection needs to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. We have two options for returning this status code, via the return code of supR3HardenedScreenImage or via the call to the original system call. Let’s see if the hardening code can even return this status code?

static NTSTATUS supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus(int rc) { if (rc == VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH) return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT; return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; }

It turns out that yes, the supR3HardenedScreenImage function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH then supR3HardenedScreenImage would return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. Therefore, what sets VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH?

This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the rtldrPEOpen API. This is reachable via RTLdrOpenWithReader which is called by the supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle function which itself is called by supR3HardenedScreenImage.

To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as AnyCPU, it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the dumpbin utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the size of code field in the optional header.

C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data

Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as AnyCPU and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the FlatImageLayout class and thus get code execution.

The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via LoadLibrary, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker.

There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the Dynamic Code Security or the UMCI options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely.

VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT from the supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups.

Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes

If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable?

Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the FlatImageLayout option by getting NtCreateSection to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the NtCreateSection hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file.

For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to NtCreateSection. We need to be able to induce the STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it.

We can write a simple test harness to call NtCreateSection first with the file, then if that fails with STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT call Assembly::Load passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually.

I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then NtCreateSection will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly.

This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled UMCI or the Dynamic Code Security option which blocks this attack. The Dynamic Code Security option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of Assembly::Load it might result in breaking important applications.

However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable UMCI but doesn’t enable Dynamic Code Security.

To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to UnregisterFunction:

using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } }

Modify the resulting assembly to remove the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the /unregister option to run the UnregisterFunction, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges.

C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister

In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI flag set, which represents:

WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG

Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by WldpGetLockdownPolicy on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement.

For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code.

For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that WerSecureFault.exe loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges.

Reporting to Microsoft

Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing.

I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the Dynamic Code Policy that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead.

However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling Dynamic Code Policy blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting.

The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following:

DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); }

The use of WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable.

Conclusions

As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake.

Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.

Title: BADBOX 3.0 Exposed: Massive Botnet Hides Ad Fraud Inside Android TV Boxes
Context: Researchers first discovered the malware in 2023, when they found low-cost Android devices with a backdoor already installed in their firmware
Full Text:
BADBOX 3.0 returns with 40 billion daily ad requests, turning infected TV boxes into fraud machines

The BADBOX botnet is back, and its latest version has reached a scale that makes previous ad fraud operations look relatively small. Researchers from HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research team have uncovered BADBOX 3.0, a large-scale operation that uses infected Android-based TV boxes and other low-cost consumer devices to generate billions of fraudulent advertising requests every day.

“At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform. BADBOX 3.0’s volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years’ worth of published Satori investigations combined.” reads the report published by Human.

“BADBOX 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that HUMAN researchers recognized from BADBOX and BADBOX 2.0.”

According to the investigation, the operation peaked at around 40 billion bid requests per day, accounting for more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by HUMAN’s Defense Platform. That’s more than three times the volume attributed to VASTFLUX, the previous record holder.

The latest findings show that the operators haven’t simply rebuilt the previous botnet. They’ve expanded its capabilities by combining advertising fraud with the abuse of residential proxy networks, using the same compromised devices for both activities.

“The investigation began with a backdoor packaged as a system application with two hardcoded endpoints.” continues the report. “One endpoint retrieves the list of modules to load in the background, and the second handles logging.”

BADBOX 3.0 primarily targets inexpensive, off-brand Android devices, including TV boxes, smartphones and tablets running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP). Some of these devices reportedly arrive with backdoors already installed, allowing attackers to gain privileged access and install additional malicious components.

The advertising fraud works by running video ads in hidden windows. The infected device plays the ads in the background, while the malware generates advertising requests that impersonate legitimate connected TV applications. Advertisers and advertising platforms therefore receive what appears to be genuine traffic from popular streaming services, even though the applications being impersonated aren’t actually running on the infected devices.

“Modules delivered through BADBOX 3.0 mimic video ad software development kits (SDKs) and render the ads in a hidden window, so the ad plays on the device while the screen shows nothing unusual.” HUMAN researchers report. “The resulting bid requests present themselves as coming from well-known, legitimate CTV apps that the threat actors impersonated to route their traffic. “

The investigation also uncovered another revenue stream. The malware silently enrolls infected devices in residential proxy networks, turning their owners’ internet connections into infrastructure that third parties can rent and use.

Researchers identified 11 such networks, including ten commercially available services and PXYEDGE, a network allegedly operated by the same threat actors behind the BADBOX campaigns.

“One of those networks is PXYEDGE, the rebranded successor to the IpMoYu network exposed in BADBOX 2.0.” the report states. “Not all of the operation’s ad fraud requires an infected device: HUMAN also observed spoofed server-side ad insertion (SSAI) traffic monetized through many of the same supply paths.”

The device owner unknowingly provides the bandwidth and residential IP address, while someone else monetizes that access.

This creates a problem that extends beyond advertising fraud. Residential proxies can help criminals conceal the origin of their activities, making it harder to identify attacks involving account takeovers, fake account creation, payment card fraud and other forms of abuse.

The report also establishes a connection between PXYEDGE and IpMoYu, the residential proxy network previously exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation. Researchers found overlapping infrastructure, proxy modules and task servers, concluding that PXYEDGE is likely IpMoYu operating under a different name. They also observed approximately 340,000 unique connections across monitored services, while the network advertised around 200,000 available nodes.

“The eleventh network is PXYEDGE, operated by the threat actors themselves and described below.” Human states. “Enrolling a device in these networks turns the owner’s home internet connection into a commodity without their knowledge or consent. The device owner pays for the bandwidth, and someone else sells access to the address. “

Another important finding concerns the infrastructure behind the operation. Satori researchers linked the BADBOX 3.0 malware catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, through several independent technical connections.

These include command-and-control infrastructure, manufacturer-owned domains, preinstalled software, device-specific checks embedded in the malware and public code repositories used to distribute malicious modules. Researchers also identified a repository account incorporating TXCZ’s name and linked its maintainer to the threat activity.

These findings establish several connections between the malware infrastructure and the manufacturer. They don’t, by themselves, establish the extent of the company’s knowledge or involvement in the criminal operation.

The operators have also taken steps to make the botnet harder to disrupt. Instead of relying on a single download location, they distribute malicious modules through public code repositories and multiple backup hosting services. Some payloads are mirrored through an open-source content delivery network, while a self-hosted GitHub proxy helps devices retrieve files even when access to the original repositories is blocked.

This approach also gives researchers visibility into the malware’s development. By examining repository histories, Satori identified an actively maintained catalog containing hundreds of module versions, including components associated with earlier BADBOX campaigns and the vo1d malware family.

BADBOX has survived previous disruption efforts. Researchers first discovered the malware in 2023, when they found low-cost Android devices with a backdoor already installed in their firmware. In 2025, they uncovered BADBOX 2.0, a much larger operation that had infected more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. Google, HUMAN, Trend Micro, Shadowserver and other partners then worked together to disrupt it. However, as BleepingComputer reports, the operators have returned with a new version.

HUMAN also joined a separate operation led by Google to disrupt XCPE, a related but different malware campaign. Researchers found more than one million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories. The operation also helped identify and take down several command-and-control domains used by BADBOX 3.0.

The researchers stress that disrupting the infrastructure doesn’t necessarily eliminate the threat. Previous investigations showed that the operators could rebuild their capabilities by moving to new servers, changing distribution methods and adapting their malware.

For consumers, the advice remains straightforward: buy devices from reputable manufacturers, check that Android devices are Play Protect certified, and install applications only through official marketplaces. Cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes deserve particular scrutiny, especially when their software and manufacturer cannot be independently verified.

The most important lesson from BADBOX 3.0 is that a consumer device can become part of a criminal operation without its owner noticing anything unusual. It can generate fraudulent advertising revenue, provide access to a residential internet connection and help conceal other malicious activities. The problem isn’t limited to the money lost by advertisers. It’s also about consumers unknowingly providing the infrastructure criminals need to operate.

“Each chapter of this research has ended with a version of the same observation: disrupting an operation and dismantling the conditions that produced it are different achievements.” the report concludes. “BADBOX 3.0 shows what that intact supply chain produces. The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record. Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name. Its ad fraud, hidden on the devices and passed off under the names of legitimate apps, reached a daily volume larger than any ad fraud operation disclosed before it.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

Title: Your Endpoint Protection Works. So Why Add EDR?
Context: Your endpoint protection is doing exactly what you bought it to do: stop malware, ransomware, and other threats before they can harm your business
Full Text:
Your endpoint protection is doing exactly what you bought it to do: stop malware, ransomware, and other threats before they can harm your business.

So why add Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)?

Because prevention and detection solve different parts of the same problem. Endpoint protection blocks threats. EDR helps you recognize, understand, and respond to suspicious activity that may indicate an attack underway.

For lean IT teams, that visibility is increasingly valuable as AI helps attackers rapidly discover and leverage new vulnerabilities and launch more convincing attacks targeting your people.

If Endpoint Protection Works, What Does EDR Add?

EDR adds the context needed to understand suspicious activity across your endpoints and act before it becomes a larger incident. Individual actions can appear harmless when viewed separately. EDR correlates endpoint activity, connecting those signals into an incident your team can investigate. It helps answer:

Where did the activity begin?

Which endpoints and users are involved?

How is the activity progressing?

What action should we take?

EDR helps explain what happened and guides next steps.

Why Does AI Make EDR More Important?

AI makes EDR more critical because it helps attackers increase the speed, volume, and sophistication of their activity.

According to the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 52.6% of surveyed IT and cybersecurity professionals believe AI is helping attackers more than defenders. AI can help threat actors improve phishing, vary malicious code and accelerate reconnaissance.

This does not make endpoint protection ineffective. It increases the likelihood of activity requiring investigation. A compromised account, unusual command sequence or misused legitimate tool may not present a simple “malware blocked” moment. Your team needs context to determine whether it is routine, risky, or part of an attack.

Is EDR Too Complex for a Small Security Team?

EDR is not too complex for a lean team if correlation, investigation guidance, and response are built into the endpoint security platform the team already uses.

In GravityZone Business Security Enterprise, EPP and EDR capabilities are integrated within the same platform. GravityZone automatically correlates attacks across endpoints. By automatically consolidating incidents into a unified, larger incident, it accelerates response and streamlines workflows.

Incident insights and response recommendations simplify investigation, so your team gains more security context without starting over with a separate security environment. This leads to better security outcomes because faster understanding gives attackers less time to establish persistence, steal data, or disrupt operations.

Is EDR Worth the Investment for a Small or Mid-Sized Business?

EDR is worth considering when the financial and operational impact of a serious incident could exceed the cost of strengthening security before one occurs.

Smaller organizations have fewer specialists and less capacity to absorb downtime. The question is whether the existing team has enough information to recognize and contain suspicious activity when prevention cannot provide the full story.

Security expectations are changing, and organizations must keep up. Customers, business partners, cyber insurers, and regulators increasingly ask organizations to demonstrate they can detect and respond to threats, not simply block them. EDR adds the visibility and investigation detail to achieve that.

Integrated EDR builds on the GravityZone protection, policies, and workflows your team already trusts while adding visibility and response support in a single, unified security platform.

Your endpoint protection works. Adding EDR helps ensure that when something unusual happens, your team can see the larger picture and respond before a suspicious event becomes a business-wide incident.

Title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
Context: ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file
Full Text:
A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.

Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

Updating the Renderer

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable

Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending

SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress

openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected

The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix.

Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell.

One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point.

The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

Title: Windows Event Log Cleared? Think Outside the Box
Context: Investigation Methodology and Findings During an investigation into a ransomware incident, Arctic Wolf found the threat actor cleared event logs, a technique frequently built...
Full Text:
The ubiquitous and dreaded “Event log cleared” event record often thwarts forensicators‘ analysis. However, new research by Arctic Wolf® Incident Response analysts indicates that clearing a Windows Event Log does not wipe the underlying Windows Event Log (EVTX) file. Instead, it leaves the “cleared” events behind; ironically, within the very file that was supposedly cleared.

The process is analogous to asking a child to clean his bedroom: rather than removing the mess, he sweeps it under the bed and calls the room clean. This article describes what our analysts found when they looked under the bed.

Investigation Methodology and Findings

During an investigation into a ransomware incident, Arctic Wolf found the threat actor cleared event logs, a technique frequently built into ransomware encryptors. This is not the anti-forensic advantage that ransomware operators assume it to be; log clearing often triggers Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) or Intrusion Detection System (IDS) alerting and is frequently the very action that allows these systems to identify an attack in progress or prompt an incident investigation.

In this particular case, the encryption binary did not execute without providing the correct password to run it. To reverse engineer the encryptor, analysts required locating the –pass <password> portion of the command line used to execute it. Triage of the domain controller showed that log clearing had affected several logs. Examination of one of the logs, System.EVTX, showed that the final log-clearing event occurred at 16:01 PST, with 104 events logged between 16:01 PST and the time of collection, 17:26 PST. These 104 event log entries were corroborated using Windows Event Viewer, Zimmerman Tools’ EvtxECmd, and Magnet AXIOM. In our testing, we didn’t identify any forensic tool that flags records left in EVTX slack space after a log is cleared. One tool we reviewed can parse events sequentially without relying on the file header, which may surface these records. However, to our knowledge at the time of writing, it doesn’t indicate whether records survived a clearing event or which records predate the clearing event a distinction that is important in investigations involving anti-forensics. Other forensic artifacts indicated that the encryptor had actually run around 12:53 PST, approximately three hours earlier; however, no evidence of this existed in parsed output from the System.EVTX log file.

The full forensic image was also analyzed for additional artifacts. A physical space keyword search for –pass returned the full command-line string for the encryptor, which had been renamed, somewhat unremarkably, to svc-host.exe. The location of this —pass artifact, however, was remarkable: rather than appearing in unallocated space (where cleared log remnants are typically expected), it was found inside the existing and allocated System.EVTX file.

The entry carried a timestamp of 12:53 PST, hours before the final log-clearing event and first reported entry in the System.EVTX. A separate, supposedly cleared, log entry also contained evidence of the threat actor’s use of netscan.exe and a leaked threat actor hostname.

Here’s the problem with that. Most forensic tools do not identify, alert on, or parse EVTX slack space. As a result, relevant data may be overlooked, particularly in ransomware investigations or other cases where log clearing is a common way to conceal activity.

Context

With the release of Windows Vista in 2007, Microsoft replaced the older EVT file format with the newer EVTX format. The new structure of EVTX files allowed for faster loading and querying. Each event is tagged with a sequential record number, and cryptographic protections make it difficult to fake new entries or remove individual entries without detection.

An EVTX file is always at least 68 KB in size: a 4 KB header, plus at least one 64 KB block containing the event data structures. The header specifies the starting and ending record numbers for the events contained in the log. The log may increase to become many gigabytes in size, but is always reset to 68 KB minimum. When a log is cleared, Windows truncates everything after the first 64 KB cluster and resets the first and last record numbers in the log. This does not mean that the remainder of that first 64 KB cluster is empty. In effect, clearing the log merely hides its remaining contents, where they remain, waiting to be found by anyone who knows to look. This means that until enough logs are generated to fill 64 KB, there will always be available data from the previous log file.

However, it is not as simple as just “carving” out the deleted records. To save space in the EVTX file, the file uses substitution templates to fill in repetitive data (hostname, event description, etc.) in each event record. Some unique data will be missing because of this, but very basic information is still available verbatim in the record. Additionally, it is possible to recreate some of these templates accurately, as the templates are mostly standardized by Microsoft.

Detailed Analysis of EVTX Files

For an analyst, forensic tools that parse data are essential to accomplishing work in an efficient and timely manner. But sometimes, manual review of the raw data is required to understand how the tools work and validate their output.

The below screenshot is the 128 byte EVTX Chunk Header (not to be confused with the EVTX File Header, which takes up the first 4096 bytes). All following screenshots and offsets are shown in decimal format.

Figure 1: 128-byte chunk header.

Analysts can speed up manual review by using a feature of X-Ways forensics called “Templates” which highlight areas of bytes based on a preset byte offset. This works well quite while still giving us easy access to confirm raw data from disk, but we still want to verify the results manually.

Figure 2: X-Ways forensics template for reading chunk headers.

The highlighted portions below show the starting and ending index numbers. (Note: all bytes are stored in Little Endian.)

Figure 3: At relative offset 8 for 8 bytes, the starting index number (1).

Figure 4: At relative offset 16 for 8 bytes, the ending index number (104).

Figure 5: Windows Event Viewer showing 104 events.

Opening the EVTX in Windows Event Viewer shows 104 events, as expected.

Figure 6: First allocated event record with identifier 2,635,913 (decimal, highlighted). Note Windows FILETIME timestamp at offset 16.

Figure 7: Last allocated event record with identifier 2,636,016 (highlighted). Note later file timestamp at offset 16.

Figure 8: First event record in free space. Identifier 2,635,767 (highlighted). Note the earlier timestamp than the first allocated event record, 2026-07-07 16:01:22.

Figure 9: Identifier 2,635,218 (highlighted). Shows netscan activity.

Figure 9 shows evidence of the second log clearing, since this record has an identifier of 2,635,218 and earlier timestamp (12:19:36 as compared to 15:00:48), even though it is later in the EVTA file (offset 53480 as compared to offset 43360). Note the netscan artifact of relevance – which took place BEFORE the clearing of the log, yet is still present and accessible within the EVTX file.

To confirm this hypothesis, analysts reviewed another EVTX file from another incident where log clearing occurred; in this case, the Windows PowerShell EVTX file. The review uncovered only one allocated record, both in X-Ways (Figure 10) and in Windows Event Viewer (Figure 11).

Figure 10: EVTX Chunk Header of a cleared Windows PowerShell EVTX file

Figure 11: Log clearing entry of a cleared Windows PowerShell EVTX file

The event log, figure 11, shows one record, as expected, with the log clearing command.

Figure 12: EVTX Record information of the one and only allocated entry, showing the log clear activity on 2026-03-06 00:54:21.

Figure 13: Last event record in file slack space, showing a timestamp of 2026-03-05 09:59:23, which is earlier than the single allocated record.

In total, there were 44 event records in this Windows PowerShell EVTX file, of which only one (1) was allocated. Interestingly, every single log entry was the same PowerShell clearing command

Systempowershell.exe -ep bypass -Command Get-WinEvent -ListLog * | where { $_.RecordCount } | ForEach-Object -Process{[System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.EventLogSession]::GlobalSession.ClearLog($_.LogName) }

This shows the threat actor clearing the log file multiple times. Whether or not the threat actor deliberately filled the log file slack space with data is not determinable.

Conclusion, Impact, and Next Steps

Event records are key pieces of intelligence for incident responders and forensic analysts. In many instances, forensic analysts are no stranger to recovering deleted data. However, cleared EVTX files pose a challenge, as deleted but still allocated entries are not recovered (or flagged) by standard forensic tools or processes, to our knowledge. Yet there are still many methods to recover these entries, if they exist. All that is required is to learn how EVTX files operate (aka how a “child” operates) and how check underneath the digital “bed”.

While we built a proof of concept (PoC) Python script to carve and rebuild old records from an allocated EVTX file, industry standard tools should, at minimum, alert on EVTX files with possible old data. As a solution, we recommend some level of recovery and notation that a recovered record is a partial record and to place the parsed info within normal forensic output.

References:

Research paper on EVTX file which covers the possibility of free space:

Andreas Schuster, Introducing the Microsoft Vista event log file format, Digital Investigation, Volume 4, Supplement, 2007, Pages 65-72, ISSN 1742-2876, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diin.2007.06.015. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1742287607000424)

Offset Charts written for EVTX library (libevtx) Specifically, the Chunk Header offset documentation can be found here: https://github.com/libyal/libevtx/blob/main/documentation/Windows%20XML%20Event%20Log%20(EVTX).asciidoc#31-chunk-header

X-Ways Templates for Quick Hex Review: https://github.com/digitalsleuth/xways-templates/tree/main

Title: EggStreme Malware: Rebuilt Under Scrutiny
Context: TL;DR: After we published our first EggStreme research in September 2025, we kept monitoring this malware family, and the development we have seen since justifies an update
Full Text:
TL;DR: After we published our first EggStreme research in September 2025, we kept monitoring this malware family, and the development we have seen since justifies an update. Documenting advanced persistent threat (APT, a state-aligned intrusion team) operations matters because these operators depend on staying unseen: once their tooling is public, defenders can hunt for it and find intrusions before they reach their objective. After we published our research, the operators revised their malware architecture and infrastructure, and the timing suggests our report was a likely trigger.

Twelve days after our report, they changed how EggStremeFuel protects its configuration. The loader’s cryptography and payload format followed 14 days later, and they appear to have moved away from the single certificate authority that once linked their servers. Based on our analysis, we assess with high confidence that the operation continues to target Philippine government organizations, with multiple victims. Based on our analysis of the samples, Taiwan is targeted as well, at low to medium confidence. The attribution is unchanged from our first report: a suspected Chinese APT group. This is a technical assessment based on the evidence available to us, not a statement about the involvement of any government.

I’d like to thank my colleagues, Victor Vrabie, Adrian Schipor, and Martin Zugec, for their invaluable contributions to this research.

EggStreme Since Our First Report: Rotation Versus Rebuild

Our first EggStreme analysis (Bitdefender EggStreme research, September 2025) described a multi-stage fileless framework. “Fileless” means the malicious code runs mostly from memory and leaves little on disk for file scanners to find. The framework had six named components: EggStremeFuel, EggStremeLoader, EggStremeReflectiveLoader, EggStremeAgent (a backdoor with 58 commands), EggStremeWizard and EggStremeKeylogger. We kept tracking the operation after we published. This article covers what changed - it does not explain the framework again, so readers who want the baseline should start with the first piece.

An APT operation succeeds only while it stays unseen. The objective is long-term access: months of quiet collection, not a quick payoff. Public analysis threatens that. Once a framework is documented, security teams can hunt for it, find intrusions already underway, and end the operation before it achieves its objective. For operators, exposure puts the whole mission at risk, so they respond by changing what defenders now know.

When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate. A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less. The EggStreme operators did more than rotate - the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together. Each change broke static signatures and heuristic detections built around the framework as we first described it.

David Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain is a useful way to think about this (David Bianco, “The Pyramid of Pain”, March 2013). The pyramid ranks indicators by how much it costs an attacker when defenders detect them. Hash values sit at the bottom, then IP addresses and domain names, then network and host artifacts, then tools, and tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) at the top. For readability, this article groups the bottom three tiers together as “trivial” indicators. Mapped onto those tiers, the EggStreme operators did three things. They rotated hashes, IPs and domains (trivial). They changed payload paths, configuration formats and a firewall rule name (artifacts). They reworked Fuel, the loader and the agent (tools). The behaviors stayed largely the same: DLL sideloading, lateral movement through file shares, in-memory execution and mutual TLS. In other words, the operators spent at the tools level and kept their methods.

Three things made this operation easy to track when we published our first article: the hashes of known samples, a payload decryption method that worked across intrusions, and a single certificate authority that led to the whole server fleet. The operators have since worked on all three.

Our first article went out on September 17, 2025. The first Fuel build with the new configuration format was compiled on 2025-09-29, twelve days later. The first loader build in the newer format followed 14 days after that, with a compile timestamp of 2025-10-13 07:35:48, and was observed in the wild the next day. No new domains have appeared under the legacy certificate authority since.

We tracked some minor changes to the agent before our report, but most of the major changes, including the infrastructure, were first observed after it was published (compile timestamps on some agent builds are earlier, so we date them by first sighting, not by build date).

Some of this speed comes from how the framework is built. EggStreme is not runtime-pluggable: operators cannot load new capabilities into a running implant on the fly. Capabilities are compiled into each build. Our build artifacts show that, from one common codebase, the operators choose at build time which capabilities to include, omit, or swap. The keylogger is the clearest example: it is missing from every newer agent build we have analyzed. Ciphers are another. The loader moved from the RC4 stream cipher (which encrypts data one byte at a time) to the RC5 block cipher (which encrypts fixed-size blocks) in a build dated 2025-10-13, and to a custom cipher by 2025-10-28, about two weeks later.

The agent’s transport differs between generations. Within a generation, builds share the same architecture and protocol, while cryptography, configuration and capability change per campaign. This design is what makes the rework affordable. Changing the cipher or dropping a module does not require a new framework, only a new build.

The infrastructure changed as well. The older EggStreme servers could be mapped from a single certificate authority (CA, the entity that signs TLS certificates) generated in 2019. Searching for that CA’s key identifier returns 32 linked domains. Newer activity suggests a move toward campaign-specific certificate authorities, with certificates and keys embedded directly in each binary, removing that single pivot point. Some pivots remain. Development servers stage certificates for domains before they go live, one development IP is shared across a set of domains, and some legacy domains reappear in the newer setup.

Above: The EggStreme build timeline shows which changes came before and after our initial report.

EggStreme Attribution and Victimology

Our first article attributed the EggStreme operation to a suspected Chinese APT group (Bitdefender EggStreme research, September 2025). This update makes no new attribution claim. The reason we treat the newer activity as the same operation is technical continuity, which is documented in the sections that follow.

Several domains from the legacy infrastructure appear again in the newer setup. One of them, mepintei[.]com, connects the EggStremeFuel activity to the loader and agent activity. Before, we tracked those as two separate clusters. Older-format loader containers, the kind the first article described, are still in use and now carry the newer agent builds, so the two generations meet inside single samples. Delivery still relies on DLL sideloading, the same pattern the first article documented. Within the newer generation, every loader variant uses the same plaintext string KERNEL32 as both key and initialization vector (IV, the starting value a block cipher chains from) in its cryptography.

On victimology, we assess with high confidence that the operation continues to target Philippine government organizations, and that there are multiple victims. Based on our analysis of the samples, we also assess with low to medium confidence that Taiwan is targeted. Readers should treat that finding as a lead, not an established fact. We do not name victim organizations, and we do not publish a victim count. This broadens the target description from the first article, which covered a single Philippine military company.

EggStreme Lateral Movement: Same Strategy, New Mechanics

In the first article, lateral movement relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself. Impacket is an open-source Python toolkit for remote Windows administration that attackers often use to execute commands (What Is Impacket, TechZone).

The operators also used the Stowaway proxy, an open-source multi-hop proxy tool that routes traffic through compromised hosts. They gained execution by injecting a Netlogon script, a logon script that domain-joined machines fetch from a shared folder, into a compromised share. The overall strategy has not changed: stage the payload on shared storage that the targets already reach, then trigger execution remotely. What changed is the mechanics.

In the more recent case, the operators staged on an unmanaged system: a machine outside the organization’s endpoint management that other workstations could still reach easily. That system hosted Visual Basic Script (VBS) files, small scripts run by Windows’ built-in script host, along with an EggStremeFuel package. The package had three parts: a legitimate executable, a malicious DLL (dynamic-link library, a code module that Windows programs load at run time) for that executable to sideload (T1574.002 DLL Side-Loading), and a configuration file.

What is DLL Sideloading?

DLL sideloading places a malicious library next to a legitimate, often signed, program that loads a library of that name at startup. The program runs normally and loads the attacker’s code with it, which helps the malicious code blend into expected process activity. Bitdefender’s explainer on the topic is What Is DLL Sideloading, TechZone.

The operators ran the script remotely over SMB (Server Message Block, the Windows file-sharing protocol) (T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares). The script copied the Fuel package to the target (T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer) and set persistence through a run key, a registry value that Windows executes automatically at user logon (T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder). EggStremeFuel: Configuration Encryption Upgraded, C2 Unchanged

EggStremeFuel is mostly unchanged. However, one significant change is how it protects its configuration, and the first build with the new configuration format has a compile timestamp of 2025-09-29, twelve days after our first article.

The earlier Fuel decrypted its configuration with RC4, using the configuration filename as the key. The newer builds use AES-256-CBC, with the key and IV embedded in the binary. The IV is stored in plaintext in several places in the binary as 1234567890ABCDEF. The key is hidden by a custom obfuscation routine and recovers to:

15c7ab53f7cfec92512844244fb09c2f07c2e9aea42b604c31fb78633248a825

Moving from a filename-derived RC4 key to an embedded AES key means that knowing a configuration file’s name no longer helps decrypt it. The analyst needs the specific binary. The loader changes, described next, follow the same pattern across components: decryption keys now travel with the build, not with anything an investigator can see on disk.

Fuel’s C2 traffic still uses RC4, with a key generated randomly on each run. Without the per-run key captured from memory, recorded Fuel traffic cannot be decrypted from static analysis alone, so packet captures will show sessions but not their content.

The newer Fuel configurations and binaries point to C2 infrastructure that includes mepintei[.]com, along with 45[.]115[.]225[.]73, 109[.]248[.]24[.]84 and 149[.]104[.]109[.]230. mepintei[.]com also appears in our records of the agent’s original infrastructure.

EggStremeLoader: New Ciphers and a New Payload Format

The loader has one main job: stealth. It decrypts the next stage and places it in memory without leaving a readable payload on disk. We identified four new loader samples soon after the first article, each with major structural changes and a different cryptographic algorithm. The IOC list shows one RC5 build dated 2025-10-13 and three custom-cipher builds dated 2025-10-28, which is about six weeks after publication.

Cipher Progression

The first build in the newer format has a compile timestamp of 2025-10-13 07:35:48 UTC, 14 days after the first new Fuel build. We observed it in the wild the next day, so we consider that timestamp reliable. In this build, string protection moved from XOR (a simple bitwise scrambling with a repeating key, easy to reverse) to RC5-32, the variant of RC5 that uses 32-bit words. It runs in CBC mode (cipher block chaining, where each block is mixed with the previous encrypted block before encryption) with PKCS#7 padding (a standard scheme that fills the last block to full length). Both the key and the IV are hardcoded in plaintext as KERNEL32.

About two weeks later, the scheme changed again. The builds stamped 2025-10-28 replace RC5 with a custom 8-byte block cipher, still in CBC mode with PKCS#7 padding. We call this first custom cipher variant A. In variant A, each byte of a block goes through a simple position-dependent transform, and the result is XORed with the previous ciphertext block. The payload path is still decrypted with KERNEL32 as both key and IV. Payload files work the same way, except that the key is the first 8 bytes of the file itself, stored unencrypted, and those bytes also serve as the IV. The file layout also varies within variant A: in one of the four builds, the block after the key holds a skip count instead of the payload size, and that many junk bytes, which the loader skips without decrypting, sit before the DLL. A decryptor therefore has to match both the cipher variant and the file layout.

Variant A stayed in use unchanged for at least a week. All four builds from 2025-10-28 to 2025-11-05 use the same algorithm, so one decryption routine covers them all. By mid-December 2025 the operators had replaced it with a second custom cipher, variant B. Variant B decrypts each block with four rounds of byte-wise subtraction, byte rotation and byte swapping, and undoes the chaining by subtracting the previous ciphertext block instead of XORing it. Both builds we have, from 2025-12-16 and 2026-05-14, use the same algorithm, and variant B handles keys and IVs the same way as variant A.

Neither custom variant offers real protection. Because the key and the IV are identical, variant A's key cancels out: every block except the first of each encrypted message decrypts with the same fixed constant (01 04 07 0A 0D 10 13 16) and no secret at all. In payload files, all of the DLL except its first 8 bytes therefore decrypts without any key, and those 8 bytes are the standard start of a PE (Portable Executable, the Windows executable format) header. Variant B looks more complex, but mathematically it reduces to a fixed byte rotation plus an 8-byte constant, so a single known 8-byte block is enough to decrypt the entire payload. For both variants, even that is unnecessary: brute-forcing each byte position separately (2,048 trials in total) recovers the payload from the ciphertext alone. In practice, none of this is needed, because both variants store the key next to the data it protects: each payload file begins with its own key, so it contains everything needed to decrypt it. What the cipher swaps defeat is detection and tooling tied to a specific routine, not analysis.

The thread through all of this is the operators’ move from RC4, which the earlier loader builds used to decrypt payloads, to RC5 and then to the custom ciphers. Every variant in the newer format shares three traits: CBC chaining, a key-scheduling step (the routine that expands the short key into per-round values), and PKCS#7 padding removal.

New Payload File Structure

The newer loader also reads a new payload file layout, and that layout has stayed the same since October 2025:

Offset Length Content 0x00 8 Decryption key, plaintext 0x08 8 Encrypted; decrypts to the size of the embedded payload 0x10 N Encrypted embedded payload, ending with the EggStremeAgent component

The key sits in the first eight bytes of the payload file, in plaintext, rather than hidden inside the loader. Because the file carries its own key, one payload can be opened by any loader build that uses the same routine: variant A covers four builds. That adds resilience for the operators, who can swap out a loader build without re-encrypting the payload it carries. The plaintext key is a design choice, not carelessness, and as shown above, the cipher adds little protection on its own.

What the Payload Encryption Does and Does Not Protect

With the earlier loader, a consistent file path and an RC4 key derived from part of that path unlocked payloads across intrusions. An analyst who had reversed one loader could decrypt payloads recovered from other environments. The newer format looks different but offers little more protection. Each payload is encrypted with a routine that differs between variant A and variant B, so a decryptor or signature written for one does not match the other. But every payload file carries its own key, so an analyst who has the file and identifies the variant has what is needed to decrypt it.
